name: Ishikari-nabe (Hokkaido salmon miso pot)
text: Miso-based salmon pot of Ishikari, Hokkaido. Fresh salmon cut into chunks, with the bones and head parts (ara), is simmered with cabbage and onion in kombu dashi seasoned with white miso, and finished with sansho. Sources trace it to a miso soup that Ishikari fishermen ate (called dai-nabe), which was served to visitors and so settled as a named dish in the early Meiji period; this origin story is a local account, not a documented date.
flavor: Sweet-savory white miso broth carrying salmon fat and bone richness, lifted at the end by sansho.
use: Winter table pot in Hokkaido; eaten as a one-pot meal of fish and vegetables.
craft: Uses fresh salmon plus ara for body, not salted fish: this is the line separating it from sanpei-jiru. Kombu dashi plus white miso is the base; sansho goes on at finish. The sources seen give no miso ratio or simmering time.
src: Ishikari City: Hokkaido's three great local dishes

name: Sanpei-jiru (salted-fish and root vegetable soup)
text: Hokkaido soup of salted fish, typically salmon or herring, simmered with vegetables such as carrot and daikon. It is seasoned by the salt of the cured fish itself, without miso or soy sauce. The MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori entry places the earliest record in Toyu zakki of 1784. Of several theories for the name, the best known says the Matsumae lord was served the soup at the house of a fisherman named Saito Sanpei.
flavor: Clean, salt-forward fish broth with root-vegetable sweetness; no fermented seasoning.
use: Home winter soup; the salted fish serves as both seasoning and main ingredient.
craft: Seasoning comes from the cured fish, so the cure level of the fish decides the salt in the pot and must be judged before adding anything else. Contrast: Ishikari-nabe uses fresh salmon and miso, sanpei-jiru uses salted fish and no miso.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Sanpei-jiru (Hokkaido)

name: Zangi (Hokkaido-style fried chicken)
text: Hokkaido fried chicken, with Kushiro usually named as its birthplace. Accounts say it began around Showa 30 at a chicken restaurant in Kushiro, where chicken was cut into chunks and deep-fried. The name is said to derive from the Chinese zhaji (fried chicken) with an extra 'n' added for luck. Details of the origin come from secondary web sources and vary by teller.
flavor: Heavily seasoned, juicy fried chicken in bite-size pieces.
use: Izakaya and home staple across Hokkaido; eaten as a side or with rice.
craft: The sources seen give no marinade or frying specifications. Origin dates and the name's etymology are retold stories, not documented facts; state them as such on a menu.
src: Ishikari City: Hokkaido's three great local dishes

name: Jingisukan (Hokkaido grilled mutton and lamb)
text: Grilled mutton or lamb, associated with Hokkaido. One account says it was devised by Japanese who had gone to Manchuria (now northeast China), taking a hint from the Chinese grilled-lamb dish kaoyangrou. Search summaries seen gave no dates, no dome-pan or marinade specification, and no regional style comparison, so those are omitted here.
flavor: Charred, strongly meaty lamb or mutton with sweet-savory sauce character.
use: Grilled at the table or at outdoor gatherings in Hokkaido.
craft: Detail to verify before relying on it: the Manchuria-to-Japan origin is stated as 'said to be' in sources, and no technical specification (cut, sauce, pan) was found in the results used.
src: Ishikari City: Hokkaido's three great local dishes

name: Sapporo soup curry
text: Thin, spiced, broth-style curry from Sapporo, served with large pieces of chicken on the bone and vegetables. Prototype: the 'yakuzen curry' of the cafe Ajanta (opened 1971 in Sapporo), put on sale around 1975. The name 'soup curry' is credited to Magic Spice, opened in 1993 in Shiroishi, Sapporo, which named its curry that and claimed to be the originator. Another source credits a shop called Hysteric Curry in the 1970s, a less reliable claim.
flavor: Thin, aromatic spiced soup rather than a thick roux; vegetables and chicken carry the body.
use: Served as a bowl with rice on the side; toppings and spice levels chosen by the diner.
craft: Home recipes seen simmer bone-in chicken and vegetables in water, then dissolve a soup curry base. Origin claims differ by source (Ajanta vs Hysteric Curry), so cite the Ajanta 1971/1975 and Magic Spice 1993 naming only as 'commonly stated'.
src: Nihon Sandai Curry: Sapporo soup curry
Tabitech note: history of soup curry

name: Senbei-jiru (Nanbu cracker soup)
text: Soup of northern Iwate and the Pacific side of Aomori, in which Nanbu senbei is broken into a chicken-and-soy broth with vegetables and shirataki-type itokonnyaku. Nanbu senbei is flour, salt and water baked in an iron mold. MAFF says the dish has been eaten at home for about 200 years in a region where cold-weather crop failure made rice scarce. One origin story links the senbei to Emperor Chokei in the Nanbokucho era at Hase-ji at the foot of Mt. Nakui.
flavor: Chicken-and-soy broth with chewy, broth-soaked wheat cracker.
use: Cold-season one-pot dish, eaten as a main starch and soup together.
craft: The cracker is a purpose-made soup senbei, cooked in the pot until it softens but keeps chew. The Chokei story is legend, not record. No cooking times were found in the results seen.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Senbei-jiru (Aomori)

name: Hittsumi (hand-torn dough soup)
text: Soup of Iwate and southeastern Aomori made from flour dough torn by hand into the broth. The name comes from the dialect verb 'hittsumamu' (to tear off by hand); other local names include 'totte-nage' and 'hat-to'. Flour and water are kneaded, rested, stretched thin and torn into dashi simmered with chicken, burdock, carrot and mushrooms. It served as a staple in years of poor rice harvest and is still served at community events.
flavor: Irregular, silky-chewy dough pieces in a savory dashi with burdock and mushroom aroma.
use: Everyday and event soup; replaces rice as the starch.
craft: Resting the dough gives it chew (koshi). Stretch thin before tearing so pieces cook evenly. Specific rest times and dashi ratios were not in the results seen.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Hittsumi (Aomori)
MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Hittsumi (Iwate)

name: Kiritanpo-nabe (Akita rice-stick pot)
text: Akita pot whose main elements are kiritanpo, rice sticks, simmered in a soy-seasoned broth. MAFF names Odate and Kazuno as the home areas: broth is made from chicken bones, with Hinai-jidori chicken and burdock added and seasoned with soy sauce, and negi and seri added at the end. Tanpo are made from slightly firm-cooked rice, mashed until about half the grains are broken in a suribachi, then wound around cedar skewers with salt-watered hands and grilled.
flavor: Savory chicken-bone and soy broth, toasty chewy rice, bitter-fragrant seri.
use: Winter pot; grilled tanpo are cut and added to the broth.
craft: Rice is crushed to roughly half-broken grains and shaped while still sticky. If inaniwa udon is added, boil 2 to 3 minutes and rinse off the slime so the broth stays clean.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Kiritanpo-nabe (Akita)

name: Shottsuru-nabe (Akita fish-sauce pot)
text: Akita pot seasoned with shottsuru, a fish sauce made by salting hatahata (sailfin sandfish) and aging it for a year or more. MAFF describes shottsuru as devised as a stand-in for soy sauce when soy was costly. The pot: kombu dashi, seasoned with miso, mirin, sake and shottsuru; hatahata with head, tail and guts removed, plus vegetables, are simmered, then covered and left to steam before serving.
flavor: Fermented-fish savor and umami over a kombu and miso base.
use: Winter pot built around hatahata.
craft: Fish are cleaned of head, tail and viscera before simmering; the pot is covered and rested to finish with residual heat. Exact amounts of shottsuru were not stated in the sources seen.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Shottsuru-nabe (Akita)

name: Dongara-jiru (winter cod miso soup of Shonai)
text: Winter miso soup of the Shonai region of Yamagata, made with kan-dara, cod caught in the coldest season. Sources say it began as fishermen's food eaten on boats and on the beach. The basic method: cod from head to innards is simmered in miso soup with tofu and negi, and scattered with iwa-nori at the end. Many recipes include milt (shirako) and liver. A related Sakata-area recipe uses salmon.
flavor: Rich, oily cod and liver in a miso soup, softened by tofu and iwa-nori fragrance.
use: Cold-season soup and pot served whole-fish style.
craft: Uses the whole fish including head and offal, so cleaning and removing blood and slime are the quality control points; the sources seen did not specify method. Sake lees appear in some prepared sets.

name: Harako-meshi (salmon and ikura rice of Watari)
text: Miyagi rice dish in which rice is cooked in the simmering liquid of salmon and topped with the salmon and ikura (salmon roe). A tradition holds that fishermen of the Watari area presented it to Date Masamune, who liked it. The standard home method: slice salmon thinly, simmer 2 to 3 minutes in a seasoned liquid, put rice and the strained liquid in the cooker, then lay salmon over and mix at serving.
flavor: Salmon-stock rice, tender salmon, bursting roe; autumn dish.
use: Seasonal dish for the autumn salmon run in Miyagi; served as a main bowl.
craft: Cooking the rice in the salmon liquid is the key step; salmon is cooked briefly to stay tender. Roe handling (marinade) is not specified in the results seen. Date Masamune link is tradition, not documented.

name: Dobu-jiru (monkfish liver miso stew)
text: Fishermen's monkfish (anko) stew of the coast from northern Ibaraki to southern Fukushima. Said to have started with northern Ibaraki fishermen cooking on board in days when anko was not generally eaten as food; no water is added, since the stew is made from the fish, vegetables and miso. The anko liver is stir-fried first, sake and miso are added, then daikon, carrot, hakusai and the rest are simmered. 'Dobu' has several etymologies: 'everything', or the cloudy color of doburoku.
flavor: Thick, liver-rich, miso-driven stew without added water.
use: Winter fishermen's dish and now a restaurant specialty of Ibaraki and Fukushima; anko-nabe is at its peak in winter.
craft: Anko liver (an-kimo) is fried first and dissolved into sake and miso as the base, hence no dashi or water is required. One Mito restaurant seasons its dobu-jiru with a house grilled miso.

name: Shimotsukare (Tochigi salmon head and daikon simmer)
text: Tochigi dish simmered from salmon head, roasted soybeans, daikon and carrot grated on an oni-oroshi (coarse grater), abura-age and sake lees. A Hatsuuma (first horse day) ritual food. MAFF's Ibaraki entry (also called sumitsukare) describes it as made in western Ibaraki from the leftover New Year salmon head, the beans left from Setsubun, and root vegetables, simmered with sake lees. The name has several theories, including a link to a household custom of Shimotsuke province and a derivation from pickling in vinegar.
flavor: Coarse, sour-savory, with sake-lees fragrance; an acquired taste.
use: Ritual and household food around Hatsuuma; made in large batches.
craft: Coarse oni-oroshi grating of vegetables is a defining texture. Ingredients are leftover festival items (salmon head, setsubun beans). Cooking times not stated in the results seen.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Shimotsukare (Ibaraki)

name: Mito natto (small-bean natto of Mito)
text: Natto of Mito, Ibaraki, associated with small-bean varieties. Legend has Minamoto no Yoshiie, on his way to the north, wrapping boiled soybeans in straw and finding them fermented; sources disagree on the date, giving 1083 or 1038. Commercial production grew in the Meiji period, and Tengu Natto is regarded as a pioneer maker. When the Mito railway opened in 1889, natto sold on the station platforms and Mito became known as a natto town.
flavor: Small beans, fine texture, strong ferment aroma.
use: Table staple on rice; ingredient in Ibaraki local dishes.
craft: Associated with straw-wrapped (waradzuto) form in the folk account. Variety and process details (steaming time, culture) were not given in the results seen.
src: Mito City: What is Mito natto

name: Okkirikomi (Gunma wide-noodle simmer)
text: Gunma winter dish of wide fresh wheat noodles simmered directly with vegetables. The noodle dough is made without salt, so the dusting flour on the cut noodles thickens the broth as they cook. Selected among the Hundred Selections of Rural Local Dishes, and designated by Gunma Prefecture as a selected intangible folk cultural property in 2014. MAFF notes Gunma has many wheat dishes, including suiton and tansan manju, from its wheat-farming culture. Name varies locally (okirikomi).
flavor: Thick, starch-thickened broth, soft wide noodles, vegetable sweetness.
use: Winter household main dish.
craft: Noodle dough made without salt; the dusting flour on the noodles is what thickens the broth. Compared to hoto and himokawa udon in the cited guides.

name: Suttate / hiyajiru (Saitama cold sesame-miso dipping soup)
text: Cold dipping soup for udon in Saitama. MAFF presents Saitama's hiyajiru as a product of an udon culture grounded in wheat grown as a winter crop after rice. In Kawajima Town the suttate is made by grinding vegetables together in a suribachi, and it can also be poured over rice.
flavor: Cold, ground raw-vegetable soup, cooling and fragrant.
use: Dipping soup for udon; sometimes poured on rice.
craft: Vegetables are ground in a suribachi rather than chopped; specific vegetables and seasonings were not given in the results seen.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Hiyajiru / Suttate (Saitama)

name: Namerou (Boso minced fish with miso)
text: Boso coastal dish of fish such as aji (horse mackerel) or iwashi (sardine), chopped fine and worked with miso and other seasonings. MAFF Chiba notes the prefecture's top-ranked sardine landings and more than 100 traditional sardine dishes.
flavor: Raw fish paste, salty-sweet miso, aromatics, strong umami.
use: Coastal fishermen's dish; shaped and cooked it becomes sanga-yaki.
craft: Fish is minced by hand with a knife and blended with miso; aromatics (ginger, negi) are typical but not specified in the results seen. It is eaten raw, so fish freshness is the first thing to judge.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Chiba
Hundred Selections of Local Dishes: Chiba

name: Sanga-yaki (grilled namerou patty)
text: Chiba dish made by kneading namerou well, shaping it like a hamburger patty, and cooking it; it is described as eaten alongside namerou. MAFF Chiba lists it as a local dish alongside namerou.
flavor: Cooked, fragrant miso-fish patty, less sharp than raw namerou.
use: Cooked version of namerou, eaten alongside it.
craft: Knead until bound, shape, then cook. The sources seen do not specify the cooking vessel or method.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Sanga-yaki (Chiba)
Hundred Selections of Local Dishes: Chiba

name: Boso futomaki matsuri-zushi (Chiba picture roll sushi)
ja: 房総の太巻き祭りずし
text: Thick sushi rolls whose cut face shows a pattern or picture. MAFF Chiba names Sanmu, Isumi and Kisarazu among areas associated with its origin. It is a festive and ceremonial food of the Boso region.
flavor: Vinegared rice with vegetables and egg arranged to form a design; mild, sweet-sour.
use: Served at festivals and gatherings; the decorative cut face is the point of the dish.
craft: Judged by the legibility of the pattern on the cut face: ingredients are arranged so the design runs through the length of the roll. Specific designs, fillings and rice vinegar ratios were not in the results seen.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Chiba
Hundred Selections of Local Dishes: Chiba

name: Edo-mae tendon (Tokyo tempura rice bowl)
text: Tokyo-style tempura bowl: tempura fried in sesame oil, which gives a strong aroma and brown color, dipped in a dark tsuyu of reduced soy-based seasoning and served over rice. Stall tempura appeared in Edo in the An'ei era and was fried mainly in sesame oil. Edo-mae neta cited include anago, shiba-ebi, kisu, megochi and kohada. Origin is disputed; candidates are Hashizen in Shimbashi (founded 1831) and Sansada in Asakusa (1837).
flavor: Sesame-oil aroma, dark sweet-salty tsuyu absorbed into fried coating.
use: Rice bowl topped with tempura dipped in tsuyu.
craft: Sesame oil fry plus tsuyu dip is the Edo-mae formula. Sesame oil was costly in the Edo period, so tempura was not cheap fare, per one source. Tsuyu ratios are not given in the results seen.
src: Marubon: sesame oil and tempura stalls

name: Yokohama Napolitan (spaghetti Napolitan)
text: Tomato-sauced spaghetti said to have been created at Hotel New Grand, Yokohama, which opened on 1 December 1927, by its second head chef Irie Shigetada. Accounts say the idea came from US troops eating spaghetti dressed with salt, pepper and ketchup, while the hotel was requisitioned by GHQ for seven years. The hotel version reportedly used fresh tomato, canned tomato and tomato paste; the Noge shop Center Grill substituted ketchup because fresh tomato was scarce, and ketchup spread the dish into homes. Other regions claim origin too.
flavor: Sweet-tart tomato, with ketchup versions sweeter and more retro.
use: Hotel signature and cafe staple.
craft: Hotel original: tomato in three forms (fresh, canned, paste); ketchup is the later cafe adaptation. Pasta and cooking details are not in the results seen.
src: Yokohama Minatomirai: New Grand The Cafe
